name: Sailor Blue
lede: Sailor Blue is a muted purplish blue that Ridgway's 1912 color standards placed on plate XXI, and which our archive finds most often in paintings by Matisse and Munch.

sections.title: From Ridgway's plates to a dictionary entry
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) gives this hue at plate XXI, hue 53′, tone k, scanned from an aged printed plate and so only approximate [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records the same name at plate 44, position D 10, first listed in 1912, and the ISCC-NBS system later filed it as a grayish-to-moderate purplish blue [1]. Our library classes "Sailor" as a place-or-institution word, and the sources we have do not say more about the choice [2].

The closest named colors are [[greyish-violet-blue]], about 2.7 units away and duller, and [[dark-diva-blue]], almost the same at 3.2 units [3]. Sailor Blue also turns up, by coincidence of hue rather than any recorded link, close to a gemstone reading: azurite's classic blue sits about 7 units off [3].

A little further off still are [[dark-soft-blue-violet]], almost the same at 3.3 units, and [[indigo-blue]], bluer and duller at 3.7 [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Across our 23,781-painting archive, as photographed, a color within six units of Sailor Blue covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 43 works [4]. It leans heavily toward the twentieth century, with the 1900s decade carrying it at more than three times the archive's overall rate [4]. The earliest known match is Fra Angelico's 1420 *Coronation of the Virgin*, where it covers about 14 per cent of the canvas [4]. Henri Matisse is the strongest match, present in four of his fifty archived paintings, over forty times the archive rate, including *Blue Nude IV* of 1952 at just over half the canvas [4]. It shares a canvas with denim-colored blue far more than chance would predict [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so every number is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
